content: The following text provides a detailed overview of various studies, guidelines, and recommendations related to HIV management, particularly focusing on advanced HIV disease, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and associated complications: 1. A retrospective cohort study published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016 examined patterns of HIV-1 drug resistance following the failure of first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) in six sub-Saharan African countries. The findings highlighted the implications for second-line ART strategies. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012 explored HIV viral resuppression after an elevated viral load, emphasizing the importance of monitoring and intervention strategies. 3. The HIV Modelling Consortium, represented by Phillips et al., conducted a modeled evaluation of modifications in viral load monitoring in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aimed to inform WHO guidelines and was published in 2021. 4. WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring provide comprehensive recommendations for managing HIV across various populations and settings. 5. A study by Shroufi et al. 6. Villa et al. evaluated the use of point-of-care viral load testing to determine virological suppression and resuppression in HIV care settings in sub-Saharan Africa. Their findings were published in EClinicalMedicine in 2020. 7. A systematic review by Luo et al. examined the HIV viral load threshold for treatment failure and its impact on disease progression, drug resistance, and transmission. This review informed updated WHO recommendations. 8. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) published a report in 2016 on the successes and challenges of implementing routine HIV viral load monitoring. 9. A meta-analysis by Vojnov et al. assessed the use of dried blood spots for viral load testing with lower treatment failure thresholds. This study contributed to updated WHO recommendations. 10. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of monitoring HIV drug resistance in populations initiating ART, including pre-treatment and acquired resistance. 11. Studies on the safety and effectiveness of dolutegravir-based ART regimens, particularly during pregnancy, have been conducted in Botswana and Brazil. These studies, such as those by Zash et al. and Pereira et al., provide critical insights into maternal and neonatal outcomes. 12. Research on the clinical and operational impact of point-of-care versus laboratory-based nucleic acid testing for routine HIV viral load monitoring has been systematically reviewed, highlighting the potential for improved treatment outcomes. 13. Studies on the cost-effectiveness of point-of-care diagnostic platforms for HIV viral load monitoring, such as those conducted in Kenya and South Africa, demonstrate the feasibility and economic benefits of decentralized testing. 14. Advanced HIV disease, defined by a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4, remains a significant challenge. Despite progress in ART access, many individuals still present with advanced disease, which is associated with high mortality, increased healthcare costs, and a higher risk of opportunistic infections. 15. Leading causes of mortality among adults with advanced HIV disease include tuberculosis (TB), severe bacterial infections, cryptococcal disease, histoplasmosis, toxoplasmosis, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. TB remains a major cause of HIV-associated hospitalization and death globally. 16. Cryptococcal meningitis accounts for approximately 15% of AIDS-related deaths worldwide, with the majority occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. Other fungal infections, such as histoplasmosis and talaromycosis, are significant in specific geographic regions. 17. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is a common manifestation of CMV infection in severely immunocompromised individuals, with the highest prevalence reported in Asia. 18. Malnutrition and wasting syndrome are critical issues among individuals with advanced HIV disease, particularly in the WHO African Region. Nutritional assessment and support are integral components of HIV care. 19. CD4 cell count testing remains the best indicator of disease stage and immediate risk of death. WHO recommends using CD4 testing to identify individuals with advanced HIV disease and guide the provision of a comprehensive care package. 20. WHO recommends a package of interventions for individuals with advanced HIV disease, including screening, treatment, and prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support. This recommendation is based on evidence from randomized controlled trials such as REMSTART and REALITY. These studies and guidelines collectively underscore the importance of early diagnosis, effective monitoring, and tailored interventions to improve outcomes for individuals living with HIV, particularly those with advanced disease.
